claims.text: Kinetic trapping during rapid thermal processing governs the formation of noble-metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Kinetic trapping during rapid thermal processing governs crystal-structure selection in these nanoparticles.
Additional time for atomic diffusion allows differences in atomic mobility to promote phase separation.
Additional time for atomic diffusion allows differences in cohesive energy to promote phase separation.
Additional diffusion time promotes elemental segregation.
Slower cooling provides increased atomic mobility relative to rapid cooling.
An intermediate annealing step provides increased atomic mobility relative to the baseline rapid thermal cycle.
Standard rapid thermal processing locks the nanoparticles into a metastable single-phase state.
Increasing atomic mobility allows the nanoparticles to approach thermodynamic equilibrium.
Movement toward thermodynamic equilibrium leads to phase separation in the stated alloy regime.
Movement toward thermodynamic equilibrium leads to elemental segregation in the stated alloy regime.
Relative to rapid cooling, slower cooling or intermediate annealing will produce observable phase separation.
Relative to rapid cooling, slower cooling or intermediate annealing will produce observable elemental segregation.
The modified thermal cycle will change the crystal structure relative to the rapid-cooling baseline.
The baseline rapid heating and cooling condition yields a metastable single-phase solid solution with minimal segregation.
The hypothesis applies to noble-metal high-entropy alloys containing at least five elements under rapid thermal processing.
The mechanism may not apply when constituent elemental diffusivities are nearly identical.
Sufficiently strong thermodynamic driving forces can cause phase separation regardless of the thermal cycle.
The extent of phase separation and segregation depends on small differences in composition and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The conditions restrict the system to more than five elements, whereas the boundary expands applicability to at least five elements, inconsistently including exactly five-element alloys.
